title: Given a string s and a pattern p, find the start indices of all substrings of s that are anagrams of p. Solve it with the fixed-size sliding window pattern and demonstrate with a complete banking mini-project.
shortTitle: Challenge 2: String Anagrams (Find All Anagram Start Indices)
keyPoints: This is the all-matches variant of the permutation-in-a-string problem: collect every matching start index instead of returning on the first.
Slide a fixed-width window of size |p| across the source string.
Use a combined count array (need minus window) and track the number of zero entries as a matched counter.
When matched equals the alphabet size, the window is an anagram and its start index is recorded.
Continue sliding to the end to collect all matches, not just the first.
Time is O(|s| + |p|) with O(1) work per slide; space is O(alphabet size) plus the output list.
Each slide does constant work thanks to the matched counter, even when there are many matches.

s1_definition.oneliner: Slide a fixed-width window the size of the pattern and collect every start index where the window's character counts match the pattern's counts.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Find all anagrams** – returns the start index of every substring in `s` of length `|p|` that is a permutation of `p`.
- **Fixed-size window** – the window width is exactly the pattern length; one character enters and one leaves per step.
- **Combined count array** – a single `int[26]` initialized with pattern frequencies; entries are decremented on window entry and incremented on exit.
- **Matched counter** – counts how many of the 26 entries are currently zero; when all 26 are zero, the window is an anagram.
- **Complexity** – O(|s| + |p|) time, O(alphabet size) space plus the output list.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, compliance defines a suspicious combination of transaction flags. The anti-money-laundering team scans each account's chronological flag stream for every position where a consecutive block matches the suspicious combination in any order, because each match is a window to investigate.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
Fixed-size window: s = "CBAEBABACD", p = "ABC" (width 3)

  ┌───────────┐
  │ C   B   A │ E B A B A C D    matches=26 -> record index 0
  └───────────┘

    ┌───────────┐
  C │ B   A   E │ B A B A C D    not matching
    └───────────┘

      ┌───────────┐
  C B │ A   E   B │ A B A C D    not matching
      └───────────┘

        ┌───────────┐
  C B A │ E   B   A │ B A C D    not matching
        └───────────┘

          ┌───────────┐
  C B A E │ B   A   B │ A C D    not matching
          └───────────┘

            ┌───────────┐
  C B A E B │ A   B   A │ C D    not matching
            └───────────┘

              ┌───────────┐
  C B A E B A │ B   A   C │ D    matches=26 -> record index 6
              └───────────┘

                ┌───────────┐
  C B A E B A B │ A   C   D │    not matching
                └───────────┘

  Result: [0, 6]
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Find All Anagrams is the all-matches sibling of the permutation-in-a-string problem. The algorithm is identical: a fixed-size window of width equal to the pattern slides across the source, and a matched counter detects when the window's character counts align with the pattern's counts. The only difference is that instead of returning on the first match, you record every matching start index and continue to the end.

The combined count array technique makes the implementation clean: a single `int[26]` initialized with the pattern's frequencies serves as both the requirement and the window tracker. As characters enter the window, their count decrements; as they leave, it increments. When an entry reaches zero, that character has exactly the right count. Tracking how many entries are zero gives a constant-time match check per slide.

Because you collect indices rather than substrings, and each slide does constant work thanks to the matched counter, the algorithm stays O(|s| + |p|) even when there are many matches. The output list is the only per-match cost, and storing integer indices is minimal.

At the National Bank of India, the anti-money-laundering team scanned each account's chronological transaction-flag stream for every position where a consecutive block matched a suspicious combination in any order. Each match was a window for investigation. The constant work per slide and the linear-time guarantee kept the screening job fast even on high-volume accounts with frequent flag events.

Remember one sentence: use the same fixed-size window and matched counter as permutation-in-a-string, but collect every matching start index instead of returning on the first.
